text.p: The sight of a municipal official handcuffed and under police escort is growing familiar in Miami, a city which seems to thrive on scandal and sensation.

Commissioner Humberto Hernandez, a 35-year-old lawyer with a controversial reputation, was indicted Tuesday on mortgage fraud and money-laundering charges just nine months after he took over the seat from a man now behind bars for a corruption conviction.
"Obviously this is another embarrassment for the city of Miami. It's another tragedy," Mayor Joe Carollo said.

Hernandez, who sat on the five-member City of Miami Commission, fell into disgrace in a city still shaken by the July 15 murder of fashion designer Gianni Versace in Miami Beach and the subsequent hunt for and suicide of his suspected killer Andrew Cunanan.
While Hernandez's case will not echo around the world in the way that Versace's did, it adds to a litany of woes including a bankruptcy threat, City Hall corruption and a scandal at the port.

"I think in a weird kind of way, with the Versace murder case, it adds to the image of this as a Wild West town where normal rules are suspended, a place with more sensation and more scandal," Dario Moreno, political scientist professor at the Florida International University, told Reuters.
And there are serious implications beyond just red faces, he said.

The City of Miami, separate to Miami Beach but linked in the Greater Miami metropolis, faces a referendum in September called by abolitionists who want to do away with it. Complaining of incompetent management, they want the City of Miami folded into Dade County.
Last September City Hall was rocked when federal Operation Greenpalm snared city manager Cesar Odio and other top officials in a bribery and corruption scam.

Odio is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to obstruction of justice charges. Other charges were dropped. Former finance manager Manohar Surana, who agreed to carry a wire-tap for the FBI to trap his colleagues, is also waiting to hear his fate.
In May, the long-serving director of the Port of Miami, Carmen Lunetta, abruptly resigned as chief of the world's "cruise ship capital" when details of mispending and indebtedness came to light.
In June, sacked commissioner Miller Dawkins, Hernandez's predecessor, began a 27-month jail sentence for bribery stemming from Operation Greenpalm.

Hernandez succeeded Dawkins, who is black, in an election fraught with racial tension. A Cuban American, he won the seat with the support of Miami's Hispanic majority, leaving blacks with no representation on the city commission for the first time in three decades.
He had brushed aside appeals from some prominent Cuban Americans to stand down in favor of black candidate Richard Dunn in the interests of racial harmony.
The son of a Bay of Pigs veteran, he is no stranger to controversy. He was dismissed as an assistant city attorney in 1994 for taking on private work from his office.

After the crash of a ValuJet plane in the Florida Everglades in May 1996, he was censured for "ambulance chasing." The state supreme court issued a restraining order to stop him soliciting business from victim's families. Hernandez is one of 13 people accused in two indictments that say they sold luxury condominiums in smart Miami neighborhoods to each other at inflated prices while presenting false documents and statements to financial institutions to secure huge loans.
At least $8 million was raised, with money being laundered in Israel and Curacao, the U.S. Attorney's office said.

"What is bad about this is that it was expected. He was under a cloud when he was elected," Moreno said. "The implication is how the ethnic polarization of the city affects its politics in a direct and tragic way."
Hernandez was released on $500,000 personal surety after appearing in the dock on Tuesday afternoon.

Afterwards on the courthouse steps, he said: "I will continue to fight for the city of Miami and its survival for the next 100 years. I was born and raised here and I care about this city and hope to be part of it."
